observers have difficulty determining the direction and magnitude of a vector field when it is presented in layers.

observers have difficulty estimating the magnitude of a vector field and have a bias toward underestimating magnitude and overestimating the direction of a vector when determining the average magnitude of a vector.

In summary, our research is concerned with
how to best display 2D vector data to observers in order to maximize their ability to mentally integrate the magnitude and direction.
the development of a visualization tool for the study of 2D vector field data.
the ability of observers, with no prior knowledge of the field, to mentally integrate wind speed and wind direction in a 2D vector field.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the layering effect has a negative impact on the ability of observers in determining vector field direction and magnitude.

the counter‐clock‐wise bias in determining the average direction in a vector field is a result of the human visual system's inability to accurately integrate the magnitude and direction over the field.
layering does have an effect on the observers ability to determine the direction and magnitude of a vector field and that the effect is not uniform.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we found a counter‐clock‐wise bias when determining direction, a tendency for observers underestimate the magnitude of vector fields, and a tendency for observers not to integrate the vectors over the field.
observers tend to have trouble with 2D visualization and the use of color to represent direction is not a viable alternative.

the addition of a layering technique to a 2D vector field can improve the accuracy of the observers ability to determine the vector field's magnitude and direction, and that the addition of an arrow to the vector can improve the accuracy in determining direction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the counter‐clock‐wise bias is due to the human tendency to overemphasize the direction of the vector field.
observers tend to underestimate the magnitude and have a tendency to underestimate the magnitude.

when visualizing a 2D vector field, the user needs to be aware that the average direction of the vectors will be underestimated and that there is a tendency for the average direction to be biased counter‐clockwise.
